Sunscreen Takes a Page From Plants | Trending | Labroots 
 Integumentary System 
 NOV 14, 2026 
 Sunscreen Takes a Page From Plants
 WRITTEN BY: Amy Bounds 
 Sunscreen is one of the most important preventive measures for skin cancer, but choosing the right one can mean balancing hard-to-apply zinc sunscreens with chemical-based sunscreens. To develop a natural, sustainable sunscreen with broad-spectrum coverage, researchers at Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS) repurposed a plant metabolite with photoprotective properties to test a new sunscreen on human tissue in the lab.
 Solar radiation that penetrates and damages skin can cause skin cancer. It includes UV-B rays, known as the sunburn rays, and UV-A rays, known as the aging rays. Most sunscreens protect against UV-B rays, which cause sunburns by damaging proteins and DNA in the top layer of the skin, or the epidermal basal layer. Longer-wave UV-A rays penetrate deeper into the skin, including collagen matrices, blood vessels, and nerves, leading to premature aging and skin damage.
 Dermatologists recommend broad-spectrum sunscreen to protect against both UV-B and UV-A rays. Protection comes from mineral filters like titanium dioxide or zinc oxide, or chemical filters.
 In a study published in Photochemistry and Photobiology , researchers looked to a more natural UV filter for broad-based sunscreens. Researchers developed a natural, plant metabolite-based sunscreen that protects nerve cells and DNA from damage caused by both UV-B and UV-A rays, offering broad-spectrum protection.
 Plant metabolites with antioxidant activity are known to increase in the presence of UV rays, mitigating damage even in deep skin cell layers. Several plant metabolites have been identified, but the current study focused on brachycerine from Psychotria brachyceras, a Brazilian Atlantic forest tree.
 Previous studies suggested a photoprotective role for brachycerine and other Psychotria brachyceras leaf metabolites, possibly through UV absorption and antioxidant and DNA-protecting properties.
 They then hypothesized that these photoprotective properties could extend to human skin. They tested skincare formulations containing brachycerine or Psychotria brachyceras leaf extract on lab-grown healthy skin after exposure to UV-A and UV-B rays.
 After UV exposure, the lab-grown skin was stained to visualize nerve fibers, and skin treated with the plant-metabolite-based sunscreen showed a regular distribution of free and diffuse nerve endings, suggesting no nerve damage, similar to skin not exposed to UV light.
 The new skincare formulations, with 1.0 percent of either brachycerine or Psychotria brachyceras leaf extract, also protected against DNA damage. Using a DNA damage assay called a comet assay, the plant-derived components showed minimal comet presence, indicating a protective role in DNA.
 In addition, cytotoxicity tests showed brachycerine was not toxic to mammalian cells, suggesting potential for future product development.
 This study highlights the need for natural sunscreen products that protect against the entire UV spectrum. This plant-metabolite-based sunscreen uses active natural botanical components, is produced sustainably, and protects against UV-induced nerve and DNA damage.
 While this sunscreen has been tested on human skin tissue in the lab, further studies on common UV-induced features are still required to confirm its protective effects before brachycerine-based, broad-spectrum sunscreens can be developed for use.
 Sources: Photochemistry and Photobiology , American Academy of Dermatology Association , EurekAlert!
